name: Fula (Fulani, Peul)

population.definition: Courtright's estimate for the Fulani community as a whole (not a count of speakers), 'spread across at least 19 African countries'. No method or base year given. No single census counts them; INALCO separately gives 'over 20 million' speakers of the language, undated.

source.title: Fulani Responses to Pastoralist Crisis and Mass Violence (Policy Brief 32)
source.author: James Courtright
source.quote: Fulani (“Fulbe” in their languages, “Peul” in French) are a decentralized community of 30 million people spread across at least 19 African countries.

facts.claim: Fula, Fulani, Fulbe and Peul are names for the same community: 'Fulbe' is used in their own languages and 'Peul' in French.

source.title: Fulani Responses to Pastoralist Crisis and Mass Violence (Policy Brief 32)
source.author: James Courtright
source.quote: Fulani (“Fulbe” in their languages, “Peul” in French)

facts.claim: The language is called Pulaar or Fulfulde (Peul in French); INALCO gives the double name.

source.title: Fulani | Institut National des Langues et Civilisations Orientales
source.quote: Under the double appellation of pulaar or fulfulfulde, the Peul language

facts.claim: Speakers: INALCO estimates over 20 million (undated, no method given); the language is spoken in about twenty West and Central African states. Estimates differ between sources and no single census counts speakers.

source.title: Fulani | Institut National des Langues et Civilisations Orientales

facts.claim: A language survey lists 17 African countries with Fulfulde speakers (Burkina Faso, Benin, CAR, Cote d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Ghana, Gambia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Nigeria, Sudan, Senegal, Chad, Togo).

source.title: Fulfulde language family report
source.author: Annette Harrison
source.quote: Seventeen African countries from Senegal to Sudan are home to Fulfulde speakers.

facts.claim: The community is internally varied: many languages and cultural systems, and a settled majority.

source.title: Fulani Responses to Pastoralist Crisis and Mass Violence (Policy Brief 32)
source.author: James Courtright
source.quote: the community encompasses around a dozen major interrelated languages and cultural systems and is profoundly heterogeneous.

facts.claim: Many Fulani settled long ago: in the Guinea highlands they settled permanently in large urban centres centuries ago and developed complex agricultural systems.

source.title: Fulani Responses to Pastoralist Crisis and Mass Violence (Policy Brief 32)
source.author: James Courtright
source.quote: Fulani in the highlands of Guinea settled permanently in large urban centres centuries ago

timeline.claim: A holy war began in Fouta Djallon (Guinea highlands) that created a Muslim state; Karamoko Alfa and Ibrahima Sori are named as its two leaders. Aremu (2011) gives Futa Djallon as 1725; sources differ.

source.title: The Fouta-Djalon Chieftaincy (in West African Chiefs, eds Crowder & Ikime, Univ. of Ife Press, 1982, pp. 79-97)
source.author: Jean Suret-Canale

timeline.claim: In Futa Toro (Senegal river valley), Muslims led by Suleyman Bal overthrew the Deniyanke dynasty and created the almamate of Futa Toro, with the Torodbe as new ruling class.

source.title: Futa-Tooro (Encyclopedia of African History, vol. 1, pp. 538-540)
source.author: Andrew F. Clark
source.quote: In 1776 indigenous Muslims, led by Suleyman Bal, took advantage of the weak Deniyanke dynasty.

timeline.claim: The jihad led by Uthman dan Fodio against the Hausa dynasty of Gobir (declared February 1804) led to the Sokoto Caliphate, run largely as a federation of emirates.

source.title: The Fulani Jihad and its Implication for National Integration and Development in Nigeria
source.author: Johnson Olaosebikan Aremu
source.quote: It led to the emergence of a theocratic state, the Sokoto Caliphate, which was administered largely as a federation

timeline.claim: A series of Fulani-led religious revolutions produced Islamic states across West Africa. The Macina state (1818-1853) is only named as the title of a cited book (Ba & Daget); no readable page on Macina was found.

source.title: Fulani Responses to Pastoralist Crisis and Mass Violence (Policy Brief 32)
source.author: James Courtright
source.quote: A series of revolutions led by charismatic Fulani religious leaders in the 18th and 19th centuries produced a string of Islamic theocracies

timeline.claim: French forces defeated Bokar Biro at Poredaka and a protectorate treaty followed on 6 February 1897; the author calls it in fact annexation of Fouta Djallon.

source.title: The Fouta-Djalon Chieftaincy
source.publisher: webFuuta (reproduction of Univ. of Ife Press, 1982)
source.author: Jean Suret-Canale
source.quote: A new protectorate treaty was signed on 6 February 1897.

timeline.claim: Under colonial rule power shifted to new capitals and a Western-educated elite; settled Fulani leaders were incorporated into colonial and post-colonial governments, but rural, semi-nomadic communities were not.

source.title: Fulani Responses to Pastoralist Crisis and Mass Violence (Policy Brief 32)
source.author: James Courtright
source.quote: beginning in the colonial era, power shifted to newly established capitals and an emerging class of Western educated elites.

timeline.claim: After independence, droughts in the 1970s-80s hit Sahelian herds, and in the early 2010s a pastoralism crisis reached a critical point in the central Sahel and Nigeria; the author attributes violence to several unconnected groups and says the whole community has been blamed (author's analysis).

source.title: Fulani Responses to Pastoralist Crisis and Mass Violence (Policy Brief 32)
source.author: James Courtright
source.quote: In the early 2010s, the crisis in pastoralism reached a critical point in both the central Sahel and Nigeria.

colonial.claim: Fulani live as a minority in every country where they are found, across at least 19 states.

source.title: Fulani Responses to Pastoralist Crisis and Mass Violence (Policy Brief 32)
source.author: James Courtright
source.quote: Fulani constitute a minority in every country they live in

colonial.claim: Colonial administrative logic did not fit local realities; independent states inherited borders that left Fulani dispersed as minorities in several countries (press article; tier uncertain).
In Niger 1890-1920, borders led colonial administrators to monitor livestock movements more closely, though state control over mobile herders was limited.

source.title: Livestock mobility and the territorial state: South-Western Niger (1890-1920)
source.author: Matthew D. Turner
source.quote: The existence of boundaries elicited greater monitoring of livestock movements by colonial administrators.

myth.claim: All Fulani are nomadic herders who migrate with cattle.
myth.truth: The source says transhumance is often imagined for all Fulani but in reality the vast majority are settled.

source.title: Fulani Responses to Pastoralist Crisis and Mass Violence (Policy Brief 32)
source.author: James Courtright
source.quote: although all Fulani are often imagined as practicing transhumance, in reality the vast majority are settled.
